name: Cape Spartel
label: Cape Spartel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Phare de Cap Spartel' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Headland where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean, with the lighthouse.

text.description: Cape Spartel is the headland where Morocco's Atlantic coast meets the Strait of Gibraltar. It stands about 300 metres above the sea, some 12 km west of Tangier, and is the north-westernmost point of the African continent. The red-and-white lighthouse, built under Sultan Muhammad IV in 1864, sits at the end of a cliff. It is a good subject for a phone because the tower is simple and bold. The place is also known as the point where the Mediterranean and the Atlantic are said to meet, and Spain can be seen across the strait on a clear day. The whole site was renovated in 2020-2021 and now has a maritime museum, a restaurant and a botanical garden, so there is plenty to see before or after your photos. Keep a few paces back from any cliff edge, because it is windy and the rocks can be slippery. Hold the phone with both hands, and take a few frames of each view in case the wind makes you wobble.
text.geographic_location: Cape Spartel is on the Atlantic coast about 12 km west of Tangier, at the north-western tip of Morocco where the Strait of Gibraltar begins.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops nearby, so reach the area by road via the National Road S701 from Tangier. The lighthouse is roughly 12 to 14 km from the city. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Otherwise use the default lens (1x) and accept that the tower will be small in the frame, which can work well for a sense of scale. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wider headland and a lot of sky, or for the signpost.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, look north-east to find the red-and-white tower on the headland. Keep well back from any cliff edge while you take your shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the horizon on a horizontal line so the sea stays level. Leave some empty space beside the tower to give a sense of the distance. As an alternative, find the Cap Spartel sign, which shows the Atlantic on one side and the Mediterranean on the other. On a clear day Spain may show in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white parts and the sky keep their detail. Take a few shots in a row because of the wind, and keep your elbows tucked in to stay steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and check on your screen where the sun sits before you shoot, so that it is not shining straight into your lens as you look towards the tower.

text.access_note: The grounds are a visitor site, and access to the tower and museum may need a ticket or have restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Spain can be seen across the strait from the cape on a clear day.
The wind and slippery rocks near the cliff edge are a hazard for photographers.
Drones are generally not allowed without a permit.
Access to the lighthouse tower and the grounds may be restricted or ticketed, so it is best to check on site or on the official site.

name: Kasbah Palace, Tangier
label: Kasbah Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bab el Assa' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bab el Assa nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12868692: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dar El Makhzen Palace' (84 m across).
notes: Former sultan's palace in the Kasbah, now the Museum of Moroccan Arts.

text.description:
The Kasbah Palace, also called Dar el Makhzen, is the old governor's residence at the top of Tangier's citadel. It was built in the early 18th century under Sultan Moulay Ismail, on the ruins of an English castle. It has been a museum since 1922, and it reopened after a big renovation in 2016. Inside, two courtyards have decorated wooden ceilings and marble fountains. From outside, what you notice is the whitewashed walls on one of the highest points of the old town, looking over the medina roofs and the Strait of Gibraltar.

From here the photo is not of the palace itself. You get an arched gateway and a white lane framing a slice of blue sea. One guide calls it the classic Kasbah photo, and it works well on a phone because the narrow walls lead the eye straight to the water. The palace stands a very short walk to the north-west, so treat this as a good extra shot beside the palace views.

For the palace itself, Place de la Kasbah shows its white walls and sloping battlements with the port, rooftops and the strait beyond. Dar el Makhzen's own exterior has the walls in the foreground with the bay below. Take the outside views first, and check on site before you go if you want to go inside.
text.geographic_location: In the Kasbah, the old citadel at the top of Tangier's medina, on high ground looking over the old town roofs and the Strait of Gibraltar. The palace is in the eastern part of the Kasbah, and Bab el Assa is a gate and lane just beside it.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to give you here, so head for the Kasbah at the top of Tangier's old town and ask for Bab el Assa or Place de la Kasbah. Walk the last stretch on foot, as the lanes are narrow and step downhill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole gateway, the white walls and the sea in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a detail such as the arch or a patch of sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bab el Assa (lane beside the gate, stepping down toward the strait). An arched gateway and white lane framing a slice of blue sea; the palace itself is not in the frame. The palace is not in the frame; it is just to the north-west, so walk that way for pictures of the palace walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch or lane edges on the outer lines so the walls lead the eye to the sea. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Then walk to Place de la Kasbah or Dar el Makhzen for the palace's white walls with the port and bay behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright sea or sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white walls keep their detail rather than turning pale and flat. A Live Photo can catch someone walking through the gateway.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late in the day, when the light turns warm, according to one guide.

text.access_note: The lane and the outside views are open public streets, but the Kasbah Museum inside the palace is a separate matter, so check on site before you go if you want to go in.
claims_not_in_sources: Bright sun on white walls can make them look washed out, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
The lane is narrow, so the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps fit the gateway and sea in one frame.
The palace exterior can be photographed from public streets and squares around it without entering the museum.

name: American Legation, Tangier
label: American Legation
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue d'Amérique' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Rue Amerique du Sud' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2328215993: the OpenStreetMap point 'Tangier American Legation Institute'.
notes: First US public property abroad, now a museum.

text.description:
The American Legation is a Moorish-style building in the Tangier medina that was once the United States diplomatic post in Morocco. The sultan gave the building to the American government, and the legation was established in 1821. It served as a diplomatic post for about 140 years. It is also the only U.S. National Historic Landmark outside the United States. Today it is a museum, cultural centre and research library, with paintings and a set of rooms devoted to the writer and composer Paul Bowles.

It photographs well because of one detail: the reception room spans the narrow lane on masonry arches, with an eagle crest above the archway. The rest of the building is hemmed in by neighbouring buildings, so this lane frontage is the best place for an outside shot. Stand on Rue d'Amérique and approach from the south, on the lane in front of the arched reception room. Look up to include the arch and the crest, and let the lane lead the eye into the picture. A second, simpler shot is the lane itself running back into the medina, past the Legation frontage.

The lane is narrow, so step aside for pedestrians and traffic before you stop to shoot. Inside, photography is generally allowed, but some areas are restricted, so ask the staff first.
text.geographic_location: The Legation is in the old medina of Tangier, on the narrow Rue d'Amérique. It is surrounded by other medina buildings.
text.directions_text: Head into the medina of Tangier on foot and continue into the lanes. Ask for Rue d'Amérique or the 'Old American Legation', which is how it is known locally. From there the Legation lies to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the arch and crest. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane is too tight to fit the whole archway. Telephoto (2x or more) is useful for a close shot of the eagle crest.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue d'Amérique (approaching the Legation from the south, on the lane in front of the arched reception room). The Legation's reception room spanning the narrow lane on masonry arches, with the eagle-emblazoned crest above the archway. The Legation lies to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the archway in the centre, with the lane's walls as leading lines. Tilt the phone slightly upward for the crest, and keep it level to avoid sloping walls. For an alternative, turn round and shoot along the narrow lane, with the medina stretching back into the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch or crest to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky above the lane does not wash out the stonework. In the shaded lane, hold the phone steady with both hands and let night mode switch on if the app offers it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter in the lane, and the light is softer. Try to avoid the middle of the day, when the sky above the lane is very bright against the shaded walls.

text.access_note: The lane outside is a public medina street, but the museum interior is reached only through the museum, so check the official site before you go for current access, and ask staff before photographing inside.

name: Café Hafa
label: Café Hafa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Café Hafa' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5017239: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Terraced clifftop café overlooking the Strait of Gibraltar.

text.description:
Café Hafa is a cafe on the cliff top above the Bay of Tangier. It opened in 1921 and still keeps its original look, with several levels of terrace seating stepping down towards the Strait of Gibraltar. On a clear day you can see Tarifa in Spain across the water. Paul Bowles, William S. Burroughs, The Beatles and the Rolling Stones are all listed among its past visitors, which adds to the atmosphere.

It photographs well because the cafe is a picture in itself. Whitewashed, tiered terraces fill the foreground, and the open sea and the Spanish coast sit behind them on the horizon. That gives you a clear sense of place in a single frame, with people at the tables adding scale and life.

A few practical points. The cafe is on a steep cliff with steps, so it may be hard going for anyone with mobility problems. Trees on the terraces can block part of the view, so move between levels until you find a clear gap. It can be draughty, and the place looks a little weathered, which suits the character of the photos. Service may not run in the morning, so aim for the afternoon, when the light over the water is also at its warmest. Late afternoon into sunset is the best window. Please be considerate of other guests when you take photos.
text.geographic_location: Café Hafa sits on the cliff top overlooking the Bay of Tangier. It faces the Strait of Gibraltar.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed close by, so use a map on your phone to reach the phone icon on the map at Café Hafa. The cafe is on the cliff top, and the terraces are on several levels facing the sea. Allow time for the steps once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the terraces with the sea and horizon behind. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the stepped levels in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Spanish coast near Tarifa or details of the tables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the tiered, whitewashed terraces in the foreground, with the open strait and the Spanish coast on the horizon behind. If you want a second view, the Nécropole phénicienne, the rock-cut Phoenician tombs, shows the cafe and the Marshan cliffs with the port and the strait beyond. Local signs there may use a different spelling.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line so the sea doesn't cut the picture in half. Keep a terrace level or a row of tables in the foreground for depth. If a tree blocks the view, take a step to one side or go up or down a level. For a second view, try the Nécropole phénicienne, looking back at the cafe and the cliffs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and water keep their colour and the white walls don't blow out. Try a Live Photo for the movement of people on the terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset, when the light over the water is warmest.

text.access_note: This is a working cafe on a steep cliff with steps, so check opening times before you go.

name: Grand Socco
label: Grand Socco
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'La Terrasse' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'La Terrasse' (node/6539852952): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8060947: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Place du Grand 9 Avril 1947' (109 m across).
notes: Lively square at the gate of the medina.

text.description:
The Grand Socco is the round, sloping square where Tangier's old medina meets the newer downtown. Its official name is the Place du 9 Avril 1947, after the speech Sultan Mohammed V gave in Tangier on that date. The name "socco" comes from the Arabic word for a market, and the square still feels like a meeting point, with cafés, small restaurants, shops and a mosque around its edge. In the middle is a large marble fountain, ringed by tall palm trees, small flower gardens and benches. The square was redeveloped in 2005.

It photographs well because the ground slopes, so from the top you can look down over the whole circle at once: fountain, palms and people crossing in every direction. The arch to the Mendoubia Gardens and the arch leading to Rue de la Kasbah add shape and colour at the edges. The best view is from La Terrasse, at the top of the steps at the highest point of the square, across from the police station. There is a relaxed local café there, so you can take a few frames and sit down. Keep the fountain near the centre of the frame and let the palms form the sides. Photography is generally welcomed, but ask before taking close-ups of people. Bab Al Fahs, the keyhole-shaped medina gateway, makes a good second shot from the square facing it.
text.geographic_location: The Grand Socco sits in central Tangier, on the boundary between the old medina and the newer downtown. The Mendoubia Gardens are on one side of it, and Rue de la Kasbah leads off another.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the medina or downtown Tangier and head for the big round square at the edge of the old town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole sloping square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of the fountain and palms. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the Bab Al Fahs gate or the café tables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on La Terrasse (top of the steps at the highest point of the Grand Socco circle, across from the police station). An elevated ground-level view looking down over the whole sloping square, its fountain and the palm trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the fountain on a crossing point, with the palms rising on either side and the ground sloping away below. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a second view, face Bab Al Fahs from the square and frame the keyhole gateway with the market activity around it. The Jardin de la Mendoubia gives a quieter, elevated view with old dragon trees in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain or a bright patch of the square to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and pale paving do not wash out. If people walk through the frame, take a short burst or a Live Photo and choose the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows than midday. Dusk can work well with night mode if you hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The Grand Socco is an open public square, but check the official site before you go for any café or other venue you plan to use.

name: Hotel Continental (Tangier)
label: Hotel Continental
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hotel Continental' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/359101160: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hotel Continental' (55 m across).

text.description:
The Hotel Continental dates from 1870 and is one of the oldest hotels in Tangier. It was founded by the Ben Dahans, an old Jewish family of the city, and it sits in the Medina, with some rooms looking out over the harbour. Its 19th-century guestbook is said to carry the names of Edgar Degas, Winston Churchill and the Beat poets, and parts of Bernardo Bertolucci's The Sheltering Sky were filmed here.

The best photo here is taken from the hotel's terrace, facing the bay. You get the water and the port as a backdrop, and the traditional Moroccan decor and mosaic-tiled interior make a lovely foreground, so the picture says 'Tangier' in a single frame. It works well as a relaxed stop: visitors who come for a drink or a meal in the café are generally able to photograph the surroundings.

Keep your phone steady against a wall or railing, and take a few frames: one wide shot of the bay with tiles at the edge, and one closer detail of the mosaics. The terrace is part of a working hotel, so be considerate of guests and staff, and take care, as access can be slippery on wet days. If you want a wider, open-air view instead, Place de la Kasbah looks over the port and the Strait of Gibraltar from a few hundred metres away, though the hotel will look small from there.
text.geographic_location: The hotel is in the Medina of Tangier, on the side of the old town that looks down towards the harbour and the bay.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot. The hotel is in the Medina of Tangier. The phone icon on the map marks the hotel itself, and the best viewpoint is the hotel's terrace, which you should look for inside the hotel. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bay and port from the terrace. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the mosaic-tiled interior if the space is tight. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tile patterns and decor details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the bay and port as a backdrop, with the hotel's traditional Moroccan decor and mosaic tiles as foreground detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, with the bay filling the background. Let a patch of mosaic or decor sit in a corner of the frame to give depth. For a different view, Place de la Kasbah offers a wide outlook over the port and the Strait of Gibraltar, with the hotel small in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bay to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the water and sky keep their colour. For close-ups of tiles, tap on the pattern and hold still; try portrait mode on a decorative object for a softer background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is easiest for the view over the bay; aim for when the café is open and quiet. Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter the tiles and water, but check the hotel's times before you go.

text.access_note: The terrace is inside a working hotel, so check it is open and that visitors are welcome before you go; the official site or the hotel itself is the best place to confirm.

name: Petit Socco
label: Petit Socco
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palais Zahia' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Palais Zahia' (way/358239686): middle (13 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/223986242: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Place Souk Dakhel' (64 m across).
notes: Small square at the heart of the medina.

text.description:
The Petit Socco is a small square in the medina of Tangier. Its name mixes French and Spanish: petit for small, zoco for market. It has long been the social heart of the old town, with narrow lanes feeding into it and café tables spilling out onto the paving. Before 1923 many European consulates and banks stood close by, and the head office of the State Bank of Morocco sat right beside the square from 1907 to 1952. That old bank building is now the Palais Zahia, a hotel that opened in 2017. It makes a handsome backdrop for photos of the square. The Hotel Fuentes and the Gran Café Central, both from the early twentieth century, are still on the square. The area has also been renovated in recent years, and the Dar Niaba Museum opened nearby on rue Es-Siaghine in 2022.

The square photographs well because it is compact and full of life: shuttered facades, café terraces and people passing through. It is a busy spot, so be patient and wait for gaps in the foot traffic, or go early for a calmer view. In the evening the lit café terraces give the square a warmer, livelier feel.
text.geographic_location: In the medina (old town) of Tangier, on the Petit Socco, also called Place Souk Dakhel. It lies close to the Grand Mosque and is crossed by rue Es-Siaghine.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so head on foot into the medina of Tangier and aim for the Petit Socco, or the Palais Zahia hotel. The Grand Mosque is close by and is a useful landmark to aim for. The medina lanes are narrow, so expect to walk the last part. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the square and the hotel into one frame in this tight space. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as shutters and café tables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Palais Zahia (framing the square from the hotel's frontage). The square with the restored Palais Zahia hotel building as a picturesque backdrop. Photograph from the public square rather than going inside the hotel.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the buildings straight so they do not lean. Use the Palais Zahia as a backdrop or framing element and let the café terraces fill the rest. For a different view, walk into the middle of the square in the evening and shoot across the lit terraces, shuttered facades and street life. Wait for people to pass if you want a cleaner shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a lit facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so bright lights do not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or lean on a wall to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the best time for an emptier square. In the evening the café terraces are lit and the square is at its liveliest.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the Palais Zahia is a private hotel, so photograph it from the square and check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.

name: Grand Mosque of Tangier
label: Grand Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue de la Marine' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rue de la Marine nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description: The Grand Mosque of Tangier is the main Friday mosque of the old medina, and its green-and-white tiled front is one of the most photogenic faces on the street. The doorway has radiating geometric patterns, green colouring and a wooden canopy, much of it still from the early 1800s. The minaret stands at the western corner. It is a square tower with blind arches picked out in white stucco, and green tiles and multicoloured mosaics fill the spaces between them. The site is old. It is believed to have held a Roman temple and later a church before becoming a mosque. Sultan Moulay Slimane had the building rebuilt in 1817-18, and the present mosque still follows that work. Across the street from the entrance is a public fountain with tile mosaic set in a horseshoe arch, which makes a good foreground detail. The mosque is in use and closed to non-Muslims, so the photo is taken from the street, looking up at the façade and minaret. If you cannot step back far enough to fit the building in, use the ultra-wide lens. Borj el Marsa is a nearby port terrace said to combine the mosque with the old port, Tangier Bay and the Strait of Gibraltar. Wherever you stand, keep the minaret upright by using the gridlines, and leave a little space above it so the top is not cut off.
text.geographic_location: The mosque is in the old medina of Tangier, on Rue de la Marine, just below the Petit Socco and above the sea walls.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot. The Petit Socco, just above the mosque, is a useful reference point, and the minaret is a useful landmark as you approach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the façade and minaret in the frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tile and stucco detail on the minaret.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue de la Marine (opposite the main entrance, looking up at the facade and minaret). The mosque's main green-and-white tiled façade and minaret, framed by the street with the public fountain across from the entrance. Stay in the street and photograph the outside only.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line so the tower does not lean. Tilting the phone up makes the building lean inwards, so step back where you can and use the ultra-wide only if you need it. Include a little of the street or the fountain for scale. For a different view, Borj el Marsa is a nearby port terrace said to show the mosque with the old port, the bay and the Strait of Gibraltar.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tiles to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stucco does not wash out and the greens stay rich. Take a few frames in case people walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the street is quieter, which is often earlier in the day, and choose a time when the façade is evenly lit rather than half in deep shadow.

text.access_note: The mosque is in active use and closed to non-Muslims, so photograph it from outside only, and check locally before you go.

name: St Andrew's Church, Tangier
label: St Andrew's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue d'Angleterre' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rue d'Angleterre nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1020366402: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iglesia de San Andrés كنيسة القديس أندرو' (49 m across).

text.description:
St Andrew's is an Anglican church with a Moorish look: whitewashed walls, white pillars and a green entrance gate on the street frontage. That makes it an unusual and rewarding stop for a phone camera. The land was given to Tangier's British community by Hassan I of Morocco in 1880. The first small church soon proved too small, so a larger building went up in 1894 and was consecrated in 1905. The bell tower is shaped like a minaret and looks over the neighbouring cemetery. Henri Matisse painted the church in 1913 in his Landscape Viewed from a Window.

The simplest photo is the front of the church from Rue d'Angleterre. The pale facade, the green gate and the pillars give you clean shapes and strong colour, and the street is public and free to stand on. If you have time for a second angle, there is a view of the church with the medina walls behind it and the minaret of the Friday mosque at the right edge of the frame. Keep the camera level so the vertical lines stay straight, and leave a little space around the building rather than cropping tight. The church is a working place of worship, so be quiet and respectful, and ask before photographing anyone or anything during a service.
text.geographic_location: St Andrew's Church stands on Rue d'Angleterre in Tangier, close to the medina walls. The cemetery lies beside the church.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is given for this spot, so start from the centre of Tangier or the medina. Ask for Rue d'Angleterre and St Andrew's Church (Iglesia de San Andrés). Once on the street, look for the green gate and whitewashed front of the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is too narrow to fit the front in, and keep the building centred so the edges do not stretch. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gate, the pillars or the minaret-style bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue d'Angleterre (opposite the church gate, on the street frontage). The whitewashed, Moorish-style front of the church with its green entrance gate and white pillars.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the gate up with the centre of the frame. Keep the vertical lines straight and leave a little street in the foreground. For a second shot, try the alternative view of the church with the medina walls behind it and the Friday mosque's minaret at the right edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the whitewash does not turn pale and lose detail. Check that the green of the gate still looks rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is not harsh on the white front, such as morning or late afternoon, and check the light on the day. Avoid service times, or ask first.

text.access_note: The street outside is public and free to stand on, but the church is an active place of worship and the cemetery is inside its grounds, so check opening times before you go.

name: Gran Teatro Cervantes
label: Teatro Cervantes
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gran Teatro Cervantes' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3825748: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Gran Teatro Cervantes is a theatre in Tangier, dedicated to the Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes. It was built by the Spanish and opened in 1913. The first stone was laid on 2 April 1911, and the building was designed to hold 1,400 seats. Esperanza Orellana, her husband Manuel Peña and the owner Antonio Gallego led the construction.

For a phone photo, the reason to come is the street front. The Art Deco facade, with its tilework and statuary, is the part you can see, because the interior is closed to visitors. That makes this a quick, rewarding stop rather than a long visit. The facade is tall and detailed, so it rewards a straight-on shot from the pavement, followed by a couple of close-ups of the decoration.

Stand on the pavement in front of the building and take in the whole frontage first. Switch on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the facade up with them so the building does not lean. Then move closer or zoom in for the tiles and statues. Afternoon is the time suggested for the facade. Keep to the public street and do not try to go inside. The theatre is abandoned and closed, so the exterior is the whole story here. The street name can vary, so check on the day.
text.geographic_location: The Gran Teatro Cervantes is in central Tangier, close to the Grand Socco area.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Grand Socco area in central Tangier and continue on foot. Look for the Art Deco facade; the street may be called Rue Aoual or Avenue de la Liberté, so check on the day. The phone icon on the map is right at the building, so once you can see the facade you are in position. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade in from the pavement. Then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tilework and statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can see the full Art Deco facade with its tilework and statuary, framed from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and match the vertical edges of the building to them so the walls stay straight. Take one shot of the whole facade, then step in or zoom for the statues and tile patterns. Keep to the public pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the tilework keeps its detail. If the ultra-wide stretches the edges, step back and use the default lens (1x) instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon is the time suggested for this facade.

text.access_note: Only the outside of the building can be seen from the public street, as the interior is closed to visitors.

name: Kasbah Mosque, Tangier
label: Kasbah Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue Ibn Abbou' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Rue Ibn Batouta' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/8851322559: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mosquée de la Kasbah'.
notes: Mosque with a tiled minaret in the Kasbah.

text.description:
The Kasbah Mosque is the main Friday mosque of Tangier's old royal citadel, and it dates from the late 17th century. It was built after the English left the city in 1684, when Sultan Moulay Ismail had the kasbah rebuilt as a walled district for the governor and his government. The minaret and the decorated entrance were added later by the grandson of the governor who built the mosque.

The outside is the part to photograph. The entrance is a Moorish arch with radiating geometric patterns, and the gaps are filled with colourful zellij tilework. Above it rises a minaret with an octagonal shaft, which is unusual in Morocco, where most are square. Its faces carry blind arches, more tilework and panels of sebka patterns.

The mosque is tucked into narrow lanes, so you can't back away for a wide view. The best free street-level angle is from Rue Ibn Abbou, in front of the main entrance, next to the entrance of the Dar el-Makhzen palace. From there you see the arched doorway with the minaret above the lane. Stand centred for a tidy, symmetrical shot, then move in for the tile details. If you want the wider setting afterwards, Place de la Kasbah has a broad view over the city, the harbour and the Strait. Check the view on arrival, as the mosque may not be easy to see from there.
text.geographic_location: In the kasbah, the old royal citadel in the medina of Tangier. The mosque stands directly south of the kasbah palace, which is now a museum.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near here, so head for the kasbah in the old city of Tangier. Once you are in the kasbah, look for Rue Ibn Abbou, the lane beside the entrance to the palace and museum. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrow lane, so the arch, the doorway and the minaret all fit. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look at the entrance. A telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the tilework and the top of the minaret.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue Ibn Abbou (in front of the mosque's main entrance, next to the Dar el-Makhzen palace entrance). The arched entrance to the mosque, with the minaret visible above the lane. From there the arched doorway and the minaret rising above the lane come into view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the doorway up with the centre of the frame, keeping the minaret upright above it. Hold the phone level and tilt it up only slightly, so the walls don't lean too much. For a second picture, move closer and zoom in on the zellij and sebka patterns. Place de la Kasbah is a good alternative if you want a wide view of the city and the Strait.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the doorway to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the tilework. Lanes like this are often half in shade.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a quieter moment, as the lane is narrow and people pass through. Check the light when you arrive, because the lane may be shaded.

text.access_note: Rue Ibn Abbou is an open public lane, but the mosque is a place of worship, so dress modestly and respect worshippers, and check locally before going inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The lane is narrow and may be shaded, so the light and exposure can vary.
People pass through the lane, so quieter moments make it easier to photograph.
A place of worship calls for modest dress and respect for worshippers.

label: Mendoub's Residence

notes: Historic residence near the Café Hafa.

text.description: Mendoub's Residence, known in Arabic as Dar al-Mandub, is a large walled property of about 10 acres on Mohammed Tazi Street in the Marshan neighbourhood. It was built in 1929 as a home for Mohammed Tazi, the Sultan's personal representative in the Tangier International Zone, who was known as the Mendoub. In 1970 the American publisher Malcolm Forbes bought it and turned it into a museum with a huge collection of toy soldiers, re-enacting famous battles. Much of the collection was sold at auction in 1997. The film The Living Daylights (1987) used the museum as a villain's lair. Today the Moroccan government uses it as a residence for official guests, and it is no longer open to the public. That shapes the photography: this is a picture of a historic building and its surroundings seen from the street, not a visit. Think of it as a record of Tangier's layered past, with the wall, gates, trees and rooflines giving you the frame. Stand back far enough to include the boundary and any greenery, keep the phone level, and use the gridlines to keep verticals straight. Take a few frames at different distances, and a closer one of any decorative detail you can see from the pavement. Be discreet, and respect any instructions from staff or security nearby.
text.geographic_location: In the Marshan neighbourhood of Tangier, on Mohammed Tazi Street, directly across the street from the Marshan Palace.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed nearby, so head for the Marshan neighbourhood by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Mohammed Tazi Street. Keep the Marshan Palace across the street as your landmark. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building in its setting. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if a wall or the street leaves you too close, and use telephoto (2x-5x) for roofs, gateways and details you can't approach.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue Shakespeare (outside the main entrance, facing the palace's street front). The palace's white street-side facade and entrance gate, with the Marshan hillside and the palace grounds behind it. Stay on the public street side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Include the boundary wall or gate and the trees behind it to show the scale of the grounds. Turn on gridlines and line up the wall or rooflines with them so the building does not lean. Take one wide frame and one tighter telephoto frame of the architecture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the building, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more even light on walls than midday sun.

text.access_note: The residence is no longer open to the public, so photograph it from the street and check the official site before you go for any change in access.
